summary: Discusses the philosophy and implementation of the ready line in the Host-IMP interface. BBN Report 1822 defines the interface, and this note comes from a committee working on standardizing PDP-11 local host interfaces.

plainLanguage.summary: The wire between a computer and the network box has a signal that says it is ready. This explains how and why it should work.

questions: what is the imp ready line
what happens when the host imp ready line drops
how long should the host wait after raising the ready line
subtitle: How a host and its IMP should use the ready line to recover cleanly after either one loses its place.

tldr.problem: Reviewers of PDP-11 host interfaces found total chaos, confusion and misunderstanding about how the Host-IMP ready line should behave, because BBN Report 1822 only described the IMP's behaviour and suggested similar behaviour for hosts.
tldr.mechanism: A dropped ready line, from either side, sets error flops in the host interface. The driver then throws away the message in transit and starts over, and a half-second delay lets the line settle after contact bounce.
tldr.outcome: The note gives implementors a simple recipe that resynchronizes message flow without involving the NCP. It is a 1974 recommendation, not a formal standard.

today: RFC 642 is a 1974 note whose status is listed as Unknown, and no RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It describes ARPANET-era Host-IMP hardware practice and makes no claim about later use.

sections.title: Why the Ready Line Needed Spelling Out
sections.content:
BBN Report #1822 gives the full specification of the Host-IMP interface, but its authors avoided issuing directives and described the IMP's implementation, suggesting similar behaviour for the host. ARPA appointed a PDP-11 local host interface standardization committee, which found total chaos, confusion and misunderstanding in the interfaces it reviewed.

RFC 642 makes the implicit recommendations of that report explicit, as a cookbook of do's and don't's for interface implementors. It says it was reviewed and approved by the BBN IMP group.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule book for the plug between a computer and the network box was vague, so people built it in many different ways. This note says plainly how to do it.

sections.title: The Ready-Line Plan
sections.content:
The plan has two objectives: reliably resynchronize and resume transmission after a temporary lapse of service and possible loss of state by either system, and keep host interface programming as simple as possible, which minimizes bugs and allows a small ROM network-bootstrap loader.

When the IMP ready line drops, the IMP may have lost state, so the message in transit in either direction is likely to be incomplete. Both sides must recognize this explicitly. Each sends a message intended to be thrown away (by convention the host-IMP NOP message) and discards the message currently being received.

The host gets this as an error status on two processes, one sending and one receiving. Using an Input Error flop and an Output Error flop, both set by a drop of the IMP ready line, lets each process clear its condition independently. A single flop can be shared if software flags and an interlock such as a mutual exclusion semaphore are used.

When the IMP raises its ready line, contact bounce sets the error flops again. The IMP therefore delays its "there's your IMP bit" and "ready for next host bit" signals until the line has stabilized.
sections.plainLanguage: If the line blinks off, both computers assume their half-sent message is ruined and throw it away. Then they wait a moment for the signal to calm down before trying again.

sections.title: The Driver Processes and Restart
sections.content:
The note describes the interface driver as two simple processes. The input process waits for a buffer and for the IMP to be ready, starts input and waits for it to finish. If Input Error is set, it clears the flag and reuses the buffer, otherwise it queues the message. The output process mirrors this: if Output Error is set the smashed message is flushed, otherwise the message is removed from the output queue.

The only initialization needed at startup or restart is clearing the host READY flop, waiting 1/2 second and setting it again. Starting the two processes then resynchronizes host-IMP communication. As explained in RFC 636, the ready line and error flops should affect only these two processes, invisibly to the NCP and without touching the connection data base. The NCP is resynchronized or reinitialized by the type 10 IMP-to-host message "interface was reset."
sections.plainLanguage: One helper sends, one helper receives. If either gets a "something went wrong" flag, it tosses the broken message and carries on with the next one.

sections.title: The Host Side and the Summary of Controls
sections.content:
When the host drops and raises its ready line, the IMP behaves symmetrically, and setting the error flops makes the same processes resynchronize in both directions. The host must delay transmission until its own ready line has stabilized, either in hardware with an integrating one-shot ANDed with "there's your host bit" and "ready for next IMP bit", or in software with a 1/2 second wait after setting the host ready flop.

The summary lists the required controls. The host needs a program settable and clearable host READY flop that drives a relay closure to the IMP, and a program-readable IMP ready status (not an interrupt). It also needs one or two ERROR flops, set when either ready signal is off, readable and clearable by program, and not cleared by system initialization.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer follows the same rule when its own signal blinks: it waits half a second before sending anything.

references.text: RFC 636, cited for how the IMP ready line should affect only the interface driver processes and not the NCP.
BBN Report #1822, "Specifications for the Interconnection of a Host and an IMP".
